# Weed eater doesn't cut weeds anymore

A common failure mode in small engine repair occurs when a device maintains high rotational speed but fails to transfer energy to its work. In your specific case, you have a Troy-Bilt TB32EC equipped with a 25cc two-stroke engine and a curved shaft. The symptoms are distinct: the head spins freely without binding, there is no stalling or bogging, yet the cutting efficiency has dropped to zero despite the motor running strong. This disconnect between RPM and torque output usually points to aerodynamic or mechanical inefficiencies rather than an immediate internal seizure.

The first variable to inspect is the exhaust system and air intake balance. Two-stroke engines rely on a precise fuel-to-air mixture for combustion efficiency. If the exhaust port is partially blocked by carbon buildup or if the cooling fins are clogged with grass clippings, the engine may maintain RPM under no-load conditions but fail to sustain power under load. When you engage the line against tall grass, the resistance increases. A compromised air-fuel ratio causes the cylinder pressure to drop at the critical moment of power delivery, resulting in a "soft" hit that simply shears off the tip of the string rather than slicing through the vegetation.

Next, consider the geometry of the cutting head itself. Even if you have visually inspected the line for tangling, the physical condition of the trimmer line matters significantly. As the line wears down to its diameter specification, it loses the structural integrity required to penetrate tough stems. A worn line acts like a dull knife; it might spin at 9,000 RPM but will deflect off thick stalks rather than cutting them. This creates a phenomenon often mistaken for motor failure. The engine feels like it is working because the load fluctuates wildly between light contact and total miss-connection.

Furthermore, verify the condition of the blade or the line head attachment. If you are using a metal blade, ensure that the mounting bolts have not stretched over time, creating a slight wobble. That minor misalignment can prevent the blade from cutting cleanly through the center of the vegetation, causing it to glance off rather than slice. For line-only heads, check that the spool is seated correctly against the retaining ring. An improper seat can cause uneven feeding or a momentary lock-up during rotation that you might not feel but which disrupts the rhythm of the cut.

Finally, inspect the drive shaft coupling. On curved shaft models like the TB32EC, the universal joint or the plastic coupler connecting the engine output to the line head is prone to degradation from UV exposure and physical impact. A cracked coupler can introduce play into the system. While the head may appear to spin freely by hand, that play can translate to energy loss during operation, effectively acting as a mechanical clutch that slips under high torque conditions.

If you have cleared the air intake, confirmed adequate fuel mixture, replaced worn line with a fresh gauge, and verified the mechanical integrity of the shaft coupling, you will likely find that the engine is functioning correctly but the system's efficiency has been degraded by these peripheral factors. Addressing the wear points restores the intended power transfer from the 25cc motor to the cutting implement.
